query: We are investigating a specific eutectic high entropy alloy (comprising Al, Co, Cr, Fe, Ni) that exhibits a dual-phase lamellar structure and suffers from catastrophic interfacial cracking and low ductility. The operating regime is room temperature uniaxial tension. Known failures include the strength-ductility trade-off and stress concentration at phase interfaces. Design constraints require maintaining the alloy composition while altering the microstructure to arrest interfacial cracking and promote uniform plasticity. Propose a high-intensity thermomechanical treatment hypothesis that could transform the lamellar structure into a patterned configuration, explain the predicted boundary conditions for success (e.g., specific temperature/pressure windows), and define a falsification experiment involving conventional hot isostatic pressing to isolate the effect of extreme pressure.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a high-intensity thermomechanical treatment (HIT) combining spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1300°C followed by high-pressure torsion (HPT) at 1400°C and 200 MPa will transform the lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy into a patterned, ultrafine-grained configuration, thereby arresting interfacial cracking and promoting uniform plasticity at room temperature.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with fine lamellar fcc/B2 structure, exhibiting catastrophic interfacial cracking and low ductility under room temperature uniaxial tension.
generation.intervention: High-intensity thermomechanical treatment: (1) Spark Plasma Sintering (SPS) at 1300°C to achieve full density with low oxygen content; (2) High-Pressure Torsion (HPT) at 1400°C under 200 MPa to induce severe plastic deformation and microstructural refinement.
generation.conditions: Temperature window: 1300–1400°C; Pressure: 200 MPa; Atmosphere: Vacuum for SPS, Argon for HIP comparison; Strain rate controlled during HPT to ensure uniform deformation without cracking.
generation.structural_mediator: Ultrafine-grained patterned microstructure with grain size <500 nm, where the lamellar fcc/B2 interfaces are disrupted and reconfigured into a more isotropic, defect-tolerant arrangement that impedes crack propagation.
generation.mechanism: Severe plastic deformation during HPT breaks down the continuous lamellar interfaces, reducing stress concentration sites and promoting dislocation cross-slip and grain boundary sliding, which enhances ductility while maintaining strength through grain refinement.
generation.predicted_outcome: Significant increase in room temperature ductility (>20% elongation) and fracture toughness, with elimination of catastrophic interfacial cracking, while maintaining or slightly improving yield strength compared to the as-cast state.
generation.baseline: As-cast AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 EHEA with lamellar fcc/B2 structure, exhibiting low ductility and interfacial cracking under room temperature tension.
generation.boundary: Treatment must be performed on gas-atomized powder with low oxygen content (<0.1 wt%) to avoid oxygen-induced brittleness; temperature must not exceed 1400°C to prevent phase instability or excessive grain growth; pressure must be maintained at 200 MPa to ensure full densification without cracking.
generation.uncertainty: The effectiveness of HPT on AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 specifically is not directly documented; extrapolation from HfNbTaTiZr HEA results assumes similar deformation behavior. Oxygen content control is critical and may vary with processing scale.
generation.falsification_experiment: Perform conventional Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP) on the same AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 alloy at 1400°C/200 MPa/2h without the preceding SPS and HPT steps. If the lamellar structure remains intact and ductility does not improve significantly compared to the as-cast state, the hypothesis that extreme pressure via HPT is necessary for microstructural transformation and ductility enhancement is falsified.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

As such, our alloy design strategy resulted in the discovery of an EHEA with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 structure and balanced high fracture strength and high ductility. This novel strategy is promising to solve the problems inhibiting the engineering application of HEAs as high-temperature materials, including the inferior castability and compositional segregation, and the conflict between high fracture strength and high ductility. In addition, this novel strategy also brought breakthrough to NiAl-based alloys in significantly enhancing the ductility at room temperature while simultaneously achieving the high strength. The EHEA concept, combining the advantages of both HEAs and eutectic alloys, and at the same time eliminating the disadvantages of these two types of alloys, leads to a promising new class of high-temperature alloys. Using this new alloy design strategy, an industrial scale HEA with uniform organizations and compositions can be prepared by the conventional casting method in a low cost way, allowing for large-scale industrial applications. Abstract High entropy alloys (HEA) have been one of the most attractive groups of materials for researchers in the last several years. Since HEAs are potential candidates for many (e.g., refractory, cryogenic, medical) applications, their properties are studied intensively. The most frequent method of HEA synthesis is arc or induction melting. Powder metallurgy is a perspective technique of alloy synthesis and therefore in this work the possibilities of synthesis of HfNbTaTiZr HEA from powders were studied. Blended elemental powders were sintered, hot isostatically pressed, and subsequently swaged using a special technique of swaging where the sample is enveloped by a titanium alloy. This method does not result in a full density alloy due to cracking during swaging. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed powders resulted in a fully dense but brittle specimen. The most promising result was obtained by SPS treatment of gas atomized powder with low oxygen content. The microstructure of HfNbTaTiZr specimen prepared this way can be refined by high pressure torsion deformation resulting in a high hardness of 410 HV10 and very fine microstructure with grain size well below 5

Results obtained for HEAP-S and HEAP-S-HIP samples (see Table 2 ) indicate that HIP processing had some potential to decrease residual porosity. However, this decrease was quite small and considerable porosity remained in the specimen. The fact that even HIP processing at 1400 °C/200 MPa/2 h did not remove the porosity completely can be ascribed to a high volume fraction of pores and to filling of the pores by Ar gas used as a pressing medium in HIP processing. The MA powder compacted by SPS contained residual porosity as well, and small pores remained in the sample even after HPT processing, as seen in Figure 6 . It should be pointed out that the MA-SPS-HPT specimen was broken into several pieces during the HPT process and therefore the results of such specimen are disputable. In such cases, the HPT after cracking could not introduce full deformation (strain) to the specimen. Contrary to this, SPS processing at 1300 °C of AT powder resulted in porosity-free samples (see Figure 7 ).
